newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zairean peace talks said on track in S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Zairean peace talks said on track in S.Africa.

text.p: Talks began in Cape Town on Thursday aiming to bring the warring parties in Zaire together later in the day for the first time, South African government officials and sources said.
Parks Mankahlana, spokesman for President Nelson Mandela, confirmed that the discussions were going ahead, but would say no more on the record.
"The talks are going on, but we are not releasing any details," he told Reuters.
One South African diplomatic source said there was a framework agreement on the table for the meeting, setting out a strategy to resolve the escalating conflict in Zaire.

A government source said Deputy-President Thabo Mbeki was leading a series of separate meetings in his Cape Town office aiming for face-to-face talks between rebel leader Laurent Kabila and Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's nephew and chief security adviser, Ngbada Nzambo Ko Ayumba.
The two sides have not met since Ethnic Tutsi rebels took up arms last October accusing Kinshasa of denying them nationality and of seeking to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.

The rebels hold towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda. Zaire launched a counter-offensive a month ago and opened a new phase of the war on Monday by bombing rebel-held towns. Relief workers put the death toll at at least 19.

Diplomats said the United States and France had representatives standing by to assist in bringing the two sides together, but South African sources said Mbeki and Mandela were eager to manage the meeting as a purely African initiative.
South African sources cautioned against exaggerated hopes.
"We have a problem with expectations that are being raised...this is going to be a long process," a source said.
South Africa's director-general of Foreign Affairs Rusty Evans told Reuters that Kabila arrived in Cape Town late on Wednesday.

The Zairean government said it knew nothing of the talks. It has scorned Tuesday's U.N. call for a ceasefire because the Security Council did not condemn neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi, which Kinshasa says are aggressors in the conflict. The three countries have denied involvement.
Plans for the meeting were revealed by Mandela after a regional summit with leaders from Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana and Uganda.

Mandela said Mobutu and Kabila had jointly asked to be allowed to meet in South Africa, but a diplomatic source told Reuters the initiative had come from the Zairean government, which previously had refused to meet the rebels in any forum.

The source said the idea was put to South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki on Sunday and was followed up on Monday in talks between Mbeki and U.S. Vice President Al Gore, who promoted the proposal.
Evans said U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Africa George Moose was expected in Cape Town on Thursday to monitor the talks.
